title: My 52-module FX portfolio just went live. How would you test whether its backtest is realistic?
author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
selftext:
I’ve just moved the latest version of my MT5 system, Foundation Trilogy, into live trading. It combines three strategy engines: statistical reversion, momentum/breakout and more selective confirmation-based setups. In total, 52 modules scan 23 FX pairs, while shared portfolio limits control how many baskets and positions can be open.

The backtest looks promising. What I don’t know yet is how much of that result survives contact with a real broker.

This is especially difficult to judge with a multi-module system. Some modules manage several positions as one basket, so spread and execution differences can change the average entry, the timing of an additional order and the eventual exit. A small difference in one fill may affect the entire basket. At the same time, several pairs can become exposed to the same currency move, making portfolio drawdown more important than any module’s individual win rate.

I’m not expecting the first few live days to reproduce the backtest’s profit. The sample is far too small. I’m more interested in whether the mechanics match: which signals appear, which orders are blocked by portfolio limits, actual versus tested spread and slippage, time spent in floating drawdown, and whether baskets close for the reasons the test predicted.

The live account has history from the earlier Foundation version, but this expanded 52-module configuration has only just gone live. I don’t want to use the older trades as evidence that the new version works.

If you’ve moved a multi-strategy EA from testing to live trading, what discrepancy made you lose confidence in the backtest first? Was it execution costs, different trade sequences, larger floating drawdown, or a market regime the test didn’t represent well?
